hints: Focus on counting bonds, not atoms, since every single bond uses two bonding electrons and every double bond uses four.
Look at how many bonds each central atom makes, for example nitrogen in NCl3 makes three single N-Cl bonds.
Add up 2 electrons for each single bond and 4 for each double bond, and see which total comes to exactly six.
walkthrough:
**Remember what bonding electrons are**

Each covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. So one single bond means 2 bonding electrons, and one double bond means 4 bonding electrons.

Chemical rule:
$$\text{bonding electrons} = (\text{single bonds} \times 2) + (\text{double bonds} \times 4)$$

**Count the bonds in each molecule**

Draw each molecule in your head. $\text{NCl}_3$ has 3 N-Cl single bonds. $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has 2 H-S single bonds. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ has 1 C=C double bond plus 4 C-H single bonds. $\text{SF}_6$ has 6 S-F single bonds.

**Calculate the totals and choose**

$\text{NCl}_3$: $3 \times 2 = 6$. $\text{H}_2\text{S}$: $2 \times 2 = 4$. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$: $4 + (4 \times 2) = 12$. $\text{SF}_6$: $6 \times 2 = 12$. Only the molecule with three single bonds gives exactly six bonding electrons.

options.A: Correct. NCl3 has three N-Cl single bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen. 3 single bonds x 2 electrons = 6 bonding electrons. This matches the question exactly.
options.B: Incorrect. H2S has only two H-S single bonds, so 2 x 2 = 4 bonding electrons. Students sometimes add the two lone pairs on sulfur by mistake, but lone pairs are non-bonding, not bonding.
options.C: Incorrect. C2H4 has one C=C double bond (4 electrons) plus four C-H single bonds (8 electrons), giving 12 bonding electrons in total. The trap is to count only the C-H bonds or to forget a double bond counts as four.
options.D: Incorrect. SF6 has six S-F single bonds, so 6 x 2 = 12 bonding electrons. The number 6 here is the number of bonds, not the number of bonding electrons, which is a common confusion.
